samples.text:
In some countries, many people do not trust scientists and experts as much as before. This essay will discuss the reasons for this problem and how the trust can be built again.

There are several reasons why people lose trust in scientists. Firstly, the internet and social media spread a lot of false information. Anybody can post an article or video which says scientists are lying, and many people believe it because it looks convincing. Secondly, sometimes experts change their advice. For example, during a health crisis, experts may give one advice at the beginning and then different advice later, so people think that they do not know what they are doing. Another reason is that some people think scientists work for governments or big companies and they only say what these organisations want. This makes people suspicious about their research.

There are some ways to rebuild the trust. First of all, scientists should explain their work in simple language, so ordinary people can understand it. Many research is written with difficult words, so people cannot follow it. Secondly, scientists should be honest when they are not sure about something and explain that science changes when new evidence is found. Also, governments should make clear rules about who pays for research, so people know the scientists are independent. Finally, schools should teach students how to check information online and recognise fake news.

In conclusion, people trust scientists less because of fake news online, changing advice and the belief that experts are not independent. To rebuild trust, scientists must communicate more clearly and honestly, and people need better education about information.

samples.text:
Although science has brought enormous benefits to society, there are signs in some countries that the public is becoming more sceptical about the advice of scientists and other experts. This essay will explore the reasons behind this decline in trust and suggest how it might be restored.

A major reason is the changing way in which information is shared. Social media allows anyone to publish claims that contradict scientific evidence, and because such content is often emotional and simple, it can spread faster than careful explanations. When people see many confident voices questioning experts, it becomes harder for them to know who to believe. Another cause is the way scientific uncertainty is misunderstood. Science develops as new evidence emerges, so recommendations sometimes change, but members of the public may interpret this as inconsistency or even incompetence. Trust has also been damaged by a perception that experts are connected to political or commercial interests. When research is funded by large companies, some people suspect that conclusions are influenced by those who pay for them.

Rebuilding trust will require several steps. Firstly, scientists need to communicate more directly and accessibly, explaining not only what they have found but also how they reached their conclusions and what remains uncertain. Being open about the limits of knowledge can actually increase credibility, because it shows honesty. Secondly, greater transparency about funding and conflicts of interest would reassure people that research is independent. In addition, education system could place more emphasis on how science works, teaching students to evaluate evidence and identify unreliable sources, so that future citizens are better equipped to judge competing claims.

In conclusion, declining trust in experts stems from the spread of misinformation, misunderstanding of scientific uncertainty and suspicion of hidden interests. Clearer communication, transparency and better science education offers the most promising route to restoring confidence.
samples.why: Both questions answered with clear, extended explanations · logical organisation with effective topic sentences · good less common vocabulary (sceptical, credibility, conflicts of interest) · mostly error-free, with an article slip and an agreement slip.

samples.text:
In several countries, the authority once enjoyed by scientists and other experts appears to be weakening, with some people openly dismissing expert advice on matters ranging from medicine to climate. This decline has multiple causes, some rooted in technology and others in the conduct of experts themselves, and restoring trust will require changes on both sides.

The transformation of the information environment is a central factor. Online platforms allow unverified claims to circulate as widely as peer-reviewed findings, and content that is dramatic or emotionally charged typically travels further than cautious, qualified explanations. In this crowded space, genuine expertise can appear to be merely one opinion among many. A second factor is a widespread misunderstanding of how science works. Scientific knowledge is provisional by nature, so advice is revised as evidence accumulates; however, to those who expect definitive answers, such revisions can look like confusion or deception. Finally, trust has been eroded by perceptions of bias. When experts are seen to be closely aligned with governments, or when research is funded by industries with a financial stake in the outcome, it is easy to suspect that conclusions have been shaped by interests rather than evidence.

Rebuilding confidence must therefore begin with openness. Scientists and public bodies should explain not only what they recommend but why, and be candid about uncertainty rather than projecting a false certainty that later has to be withdrawn. Full disclosure of funding sources would go some way towards addressing suspicions of hidden agendas. Experts also need to engage with communities directly, through local events and accessible media, rather than communicating solely through official statements. In the longer term, education has a vital role: teaching young people how evidence is gathered and assessed would equip them to distinguish credible research from persuasive misinformation.

In conclusion, trust in experts is being undermined by an unregulated information environment, misconceptions about scientific uncertainty and suspicions of bias. Greater transparency, honest communication and stronger scientific literacy offer the best prospect of restoring it.
